fun_fact: Its crown stays narrow and upright where most purpleleaf plums spread, which is how it became one of the most planted street trees on the American west coast.

bark_profile: Red-brown, glossy, marked with horizontal lenticels
pest_resistance: Brown rot and borers; needs airflow
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun
description: The standard sour cherry of American pie, self-fertile and hardy enough to crop reliably in Vermont.
fun_fact: Named for a valley north of Paris. Most American tart cherries now come from Michigan, where Traverse City calls itself the cherry capital of the world.

bark_profile: Glossy amber-bronze, peeling in curls — its main ornamental feature
pest_resistance: Hardier and longer-lived than most ornamental cherries
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; very cold hardy
description: Amur chokecherry, grown almost entirely for its glossy, peeling bark in polished amber and bronze.
fun_fact: It is native to the Amur River valley on the border of Russia and China, where winters are colder than Vermont's.

bark_profile: Dark grey-brown, smooth, strongly and unpleasantly scented when cut
pest_resistance: Prone to aphids and bacterial canker
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates cold
description: Long drooping racemes of almond-scented white flowers, unusual in a cherry. Bitter black fruit follows in midsummer.
fun_fact: The caterpillars of the bird-cherry ermine moth can wrap a whole tree in silk webbing in June. It looks alarming, but the tree leafs out again.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, glossy, with conspicuous orange lenticels
pest_resistance: Short-lived by nature; black knot
soil_preference: Dry to moist; a pioneer after fire or logging
description: A short-lived native cherry that floods in after fire or logging, then gives way as longer-lived trees close over it.
fun_fact: Called fire cherry: its seed lies dormant in forest soil for decades and germinates en masse after a burn.

bark_profile: Dark grey-brown, marked with horizontal lenticels
pest_resistance: Peach leaf curl, borers and canker; short-lived here
soil_preference: Light, well-drained, sandy; needs full sun
description: Pink flowers before the leaves, and fruit only in a good year this far north. Reliably short-lived in Vermont.
fun_fact: Peaches came from China, not Persia. The name records where Europeans first met them, not where they are from.

bark_profile: Glossy chestnut-brown with prominent horizontal lenticel bands
pest_resistance: The longest-lived and most cold-hardy of the ornamental cherries
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: The hardiest ornamental cherry, with single pink flowers, polished mahogany bark and autumn foliage that turns bronze-orange before settling into brick red.
fun_fact: Named for Charles Sprague Sargent, first director of Harvard's Arnold Arboretum, who brought its seed back from Japan in 1892.

bark_profile: Glossy chestnut-brown with prominent horizontal lenticel bands
pest_resistance: The longest-lived and most cold-hardy of the ornamental cherries
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: An upright Sargent cherry narrow enough for a street, with the same single pink flowers and glossy mahogany bark.
fun_fact: Sargent cherry grows wild in the mountains of northern Japan, Sakhalin and Korea, which is where its cold-hardiness comes from.

bark_profile: Young bark dark with horizontal lenticels; old bark breaking into burnt-cornflake plates
pest_resistance: Eastern tent caterpillar; foliage is toxic to livestock when wilted
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, deep
description: Mature bark breaks into dark curling plates often likened to burnt cornflakes. Small black cherries in late summer feed most of the woodland.
fun_fact: Wilted leaves release cyanide, which has killed livestock that browsed a fallen limb. The wood is one of North America's finest cabinet timbers.

bark_profile: Glossy chestnut-brown with prominent lenticel bands
pest_resistance: Short-lived; borers, black knot, canker
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: The Japanese flowering cherries, usually double-flowered and fruitless, planted purely for a brief and spectacular spring bloom.
fun_fact: In the double forms the stamens have been bred into extra petals. The flower has traded its reproductive parts for show, which is why it sets almost nothing.

bark_profile: Glossy with horizontal lenticel bands
pest_resistance: Black knot; borers
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained
description: Cherries and plums: five-petalled white or pink blossom in spring, and fleshy fruit around a single stone. Many carry a pair of small glands on the leafstalk, just below the leaf.
fun_fact: The horizontal lines on a cherry trunk are lenticels, pores that let the bark breathe. They stretch as the trunk grows.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, lenticelled, becoming rough with age
pest_resistance: Borers; canker
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; shelter from wind
description: Higan cherry, often grown in weeping form, and among the earliest cherries to flower. Sometimes blooms again in a mild autumn.
fun_fact: In Japan it is called higan-zakura, because it blooms around Higan, the Buddhist week of the spring equinox.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, lenticelled, becoming rough with age
pest_resistance: Borers; canker
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; shelter from wind
description: Branches arch over and hang to the ground, covered in pale pink flowers before the leaves. Usually grafted high on a standard trunk.
fun_fact: The weeping habit is grafted high onto a straight stock: the crown you see and the trunk holding it up are two different plants.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, smooth, with a strong sour smell when scratched
pest_resistance: Tent caterpillar and black knot
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates dry and poor soils
description: A suckering native cherry forming thickets. Astringent fruit, edible once cooked, and the source of chokecherry jelly.
fun_fact: It is the state fruit of North Dakota.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, smooth, with a strong sour smell when scratched
pest_resistance: Tent caterpillar and black knot
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates dry and poor soils
description: Leaves emerge green and turn deep purple-red through early summer, so the tree changes colour as the season goes on.
fun_fact: Nearly every ornamental cherry in a northern landscape is Asian. This one is a selection of a chokecherry native to North America, growing wild in Vermont hedgerows and clearings.

bark_profile: Dark reddish-brown, smooth
pest_resistance: Prone to borers, canker and leaf spot; short-lived
soil_preference: Well-drained; full sun for best leaf colour
description: Grown for its deep red-purple foliage from spring until leaf fall. Pale pink flowers appear against the emerging purple leaves.
fun_fact: Bred in South Dakota in 1910 for prairie cold, which is why a purple-leaved shrub survives where most would not.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown with horizontal lenticels
pest_resistance: Short-lived; borers and canker
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: The Yoshino cherry of Washington's Tidal Basin: pale blush flowers, almost white, opening all at once before the leaves.
fun_fact: Tokyo gave Washington 3,020 cherry trees in 1912, most of them Yoshino, and the United States sent flowering dogwoods back to Japan in 1915.

bark_profile: Smooth with resin blisters, becoming thick and corky
pest_resistance: Cooley spruce gall adelgid; needlecast
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid
description: Not a true fir. Its cones are unmistakable, with three-pointed bracts poking out between the scales like the hind legs of a mouse.
fun_fact: Softwood plywood began with this tree. The first panels were pressed from Douglas fir in Portland for the 1905 world's fair, and the result became the standard sheet material of North American building.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown with warty lenticels
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates shade and dry soil
description: A small tree with three-part leaves and flat circular winged fruits like elm seeds, which is where the name wafer ash comes from.
fun_fact: In the citrus family, which explains why the crushed leaves smell of it. The papery winged seeds were once used as a hop substitute in brewing.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly furrowed
pest_resistance: Fire blight; narrow branch angles split in storms — a known liability
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates drought and compaction
description: Once planted everywhere for its neat shape and early white bloom, now regretted: the branches split in storms and it escapes into the wild.
fun_fact: It was sold as sterile, and was — until enough different cultivars stood close enough to pollinate one another. Several states have now banned it outright.

bark_profile: Dark grey, blocky and checkered with age
pest_resistance: Fire blight; pear psylla
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; full sun
description: The orchard pear, with glossy leaves, white spring flowers and blocky, checkered bark on old trunks.
fun_fact: Pear wood is dense and even-grained enough for woodwind instruments and engraving blocks, and it was long the standard for drawing instruments.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, becoming lightly furrowed
pest_resistance: Better fireblight resistance than Callery pear; does not seed invasively
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates urban conditions
description: A compact Korean pear with glossy leaves that turn red in autumn, white spring flowers, and small, hard, inedible fruit.
fun_fact: Pear trees can live for centuries: the Endicott pear, planted in Massachusetts around 1630, still bears fruit.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: Most street pears are Callery selections: white blossom very early in spring with a smell many people find unpleasant, glossy leaves held late into autumn, and seedlings that spread into old fields.
fun_fact: Pears are in the rose family, like apples, cherries, hawthorns and serviceberries — which is why their five-petalled blossoms look so alike.

bark_profile: Pale ashy grey, flaking in loose plates
pest_resistance: Spongy moth; slow to establish after transplant
soil_preference: Deep, well-drained, acid
description: A long-lived native oak with rounded, finger-like leaf lobes, pale ashy bark that flakes in loose plates, and sweet acorns that ripen in a single year.
fun_fact: Its wood is watertight: the pores are plugged with natural growths, which is why whiskey and wine barrels are made of white oak and not red.

bark_profile: Flaking and curling on branches, ridged on the trunk
pest_resistance: Chlorosis on alkaline soil
soil_preference: Wet to moist, acid; tolerates poor drainage
description: A white oak of wet ground, with leaves dark green above and silvery beneath, and bark that flakes and curls on young branches.
fun_fact: Its acorns dangle in pairs on stalks up to four inches long. Most oak acorns sit tight against the twig.

bark_profile: Dark grey with pale inner bark showing in the fissures
pest_resistance: Spongy moth
soil_preference: Dry, sandy, acid
description: Deeply cut, bristle-tipped leaves that turn brilliant scarlet late in the season and hold on well into winter.
fun_fact: It is the official tree of Washington, DC.

bark_profile: Dark grey-brown, shallowly furrowed
pest_resistance: Fewer problems than pin oak on alkaline soil
soil_preference: Dry, sandy, acidic; drought tolerant
description: Closely resembles pin oak but tolerates dry and alkaline ground far better. Deep red fall colour that holds late.
fun_fact: A northern oak of dry sandy ground, closely related to pin oak but holding its dead lower branches rather than dropping them.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, darkening and furrowing with age
pest_resistance: Well outside its hardiness range here
soil_preference: Well-drained, sandy
description: A southern laurel oak with narrow, nearly untoothed leaves. Well outside its natural range here.
fun_fact: A southern oak that holds its leaves through winter and drops them only as the new ones push out.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly ridged
pest_resistance: Spongy moth
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates dry sites
description: An oak with unlobed, laurel-like leaves that surprise anyone expecting an oak. Its wood was once split for roof shingles.
fun_fact: It is a red oak all the same: its acorns take two years to ripen, and each leaf ends in a single bristle, the one oak feature it kept.

bark_profile: Thick, deeply ridged, corky
pest_resistance: Very few; the most fire and drought resistant oak here
soil_preference: Wide range including alkaline and clay
description: Enormous acorns in shaggy, fringed cups. Thick corky bark makes it the most fire-resistant oak of the prairie edge.
fun_fact: A bur oak seedling puts its energy underground first: in its first season the taproot can reach four feet down while the shoot stands only inches tall. That head start is how it survives drought and fire.

bark_profile: Light grey, flaking in loose scales
pest_resistance: Few known problems; well outside its range here
soil_preference: Moist bottomland; tolerates wet
description: A southern bottomland oak with large, coarsely scalloped leaves and sweet acorns favoured by wildlife.
fun_fact: Named for André Michaux, the French botanist who catalogued much of eastern North America's flora in the 1780s and 90s.

bark_profile: Flaky, ashy grey, breaking into thin plates
pest_resistance: Few known problems
soil_preference: Prefers limestone and alkaline soil
description: Chinkapin oak, with narrow chestnut-like leaves edged in sharp even teeth. Prefers limestone soils.
fun_fact: Squirrels strip it first. Its acorns carry far less tannin than most, sweet enough to eat raw, which no red oak acorn ever is.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown, shallowly ridged with age
pest_resistance: Chlorosis on alkaline soil is common and disfiguring
soil_preference: Moist, acid; tolerates wet ground
description: Lower branches sweep distinctly downward while the upper ones rise — a silhouette no other oak shares. Deeply cut leaves turn bronze-red.
fun_fact: Palustris means "of the marsh": in the wild it grows on river floodplains. Its small acorns are a favourite of wood ducks, and wildlife managers flood pin oak stands in autumn to feed ducks on their way south.

bark_profile: Very thick, deeply furrowed into rugged blocky ridges
pest_resistance: Spongy moth
soil_preference: Dry rocky ridges, acid; drought tolerant
description: Chestnut oak of dry rocky ridges, with deeply furrowed blocky bark and wavy-edged leaves. Now usually called Quercus montana.
fun_fact: The bark is the thickest and most deeply ridged of any eastern oak, and was stripped by the ton for tannin before synthetic tanning arrived.

bark_profile: Deeply fissured grey-brown in a fine network
pest_resistance: Powdery mildew is routine and mostly cosmetic
soil_preference: Deep, fertile; tolerates clay
description: The English oak of parkland and literature, with short-stalked leaves, long-stalked acorns, and a broad spreading crown when open-grown.
fun_fact: The oak of English history and the Royal Navy. A single ship of the line took around two thousand mature trees.

bark_profile: Deeply fissured grey-brown in a fine network
pest_resistance: Powdery mildew is routine and mostly cosmetic
soil_preference: Deep, fertile; tolerates clay
description: A columnar form of English oak, with branches held tight to the trunk so the tree stands like a closed umbrella. Its leaves have the small ear-like lobes at the base that mark English oak.
fun_fact: Its acorns mostly grow into the ordinary broad, spreading English oak, so every narrow one you see is a graft.

bark_profile: Grey with flat-topped shiny ridges, striped down the trunk
pest_resistance: Spongy moth; oak wilt
soil_preference: Well-drained, acid; fast for an oak
description: A native oak with pointed, bristle-tipped leaf lobes and fat acorns wearing a flat, beret-like cap. On the trunk, look for smooth, shiny stripes running down between the ridges.
fun_fact: Red oak grows faster than white and its wood is porous end to end — you can blow bubbles through a short length of it, which is why it will not hold liquid.

bark_profile: Near-black, blocky, with bright orange inner bark
pest_resistance: Spongy moth; oak wilt
soil_preference: Dry, sandy, acid; drought tolerant
description: Inner bark is bright orange-yellow and was once used as a dye. Leaves are glossy above with rusty hairs in the vein axils beneath.
fun_fact: That dye had a name and a trade: quercitron, shipped out of American ports by the ton through the 1800s to colour European cloth.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly ridged
pest_resistance: Good mildew resistance for a hybrid oak
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates urban soils
description: A narrow columnar hybrid of English and white oak, planted where an oak is wanted but there is no room for a crown.
fun_fact: Bimundorum means 'of two worlds' — one parent European, one American, which is exactly what it is.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly furrowed
pest_resistance: Good mildew resistance; tolerates alkaline soil
soil_preference: Wide range including alkaline and compacted
description: An upright hybrid oak bred for street planting, holding a narrow pyramidal shape without pruning.
fun_fact: A cross between English oak and swamp white oak, named for George Ware, the Morton Arboretum researcher who bred it.

bark_profile: Dark grey-brown, peeling to reveal orange inner bark
pest_resistance: Few pests, which is part of the problem. Invasive in Vermont
soil_preference: Very adaptable; shades out native seedlings
description: A Class B noxious weed in Vermont. Twigs often end in a short thorn, and the black berries hang on into winter, long after the leaves have gone.
fun_fact: Sold as a hedge plant for a century before anyone noticed it was taking over the understorey. Birds spread the seed, and the berries are a strong laxative — which names it.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: Both common and glossy buckthorn are invasive in Vermont. Look for dark berries hanging on into winter and, on common buckthorn, a short thorn at the tip of many twigs.
fun_fact: Buckthorn leafs out earlier and holds its leaves later than almost any native, which is how it starves out everything growing beneath it.

bark_profile: Deeply furrowed into a rope-like interlacing pattern
pest_resistance: Locust borer; leaf miner
soil_preference: Poor, dry ground; fixes nitrogen, suckers freely
description: Deeply furrowed rope-like bark, paired thorns at each bud, and hanging chains of intensely fragrant white flowers in June.
fun_fact: The heartwood resists rot for decades in ground contact, so it was the standard for fence posts and for the trunnels that pinned ships together.

bark_profile: Deeply furrowed into a rope-like interlacing pattern
pest_resistance: Locust borer; leaf miner
soil_preference: Poor, dry ground; fixes nitrogen, suckers freely
description: Rose-purple pea flowers in hanging clusters instead of the white of the species, and bronze-tinted new growth. Invasive in Vermont.
fun_fact: Black locust is native to the Appalachians and the Ozarks and to nowhere else. Everywhere beyond that, Vermont included, it is an import that escaped — a native tree can still be invasive three hundred miles from home.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, deeply furrowed and criss-crossed
pest_resistance: Canker; borers; brittle in storms
soil_preference: Wet ground; tolerates flooding
description: A large European willow with narrow silvery leaves. Its wood is light, tough and shock-resistant.
fun_fact: Cricket bats are made from a form of it, the cricket-bat willow, whose light, tough wood absorbs the shock of the ball.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, deeply ridged; young shoots bright golden-yellow
pest_resistance: Canker; borers; brittle in storms
soil_preference: Wet ground; tolerates flooding
description: Golden-yellow winter shoots hanging in long curtains to the ground. Fast, brittle, and thirsty enough to find drains.
fun_fact: Half its parentage is the Chinese weeping willow, which Linnaeus named Salix babylonica after the willows of Babylon in Psalm 137, though those were probably poplars.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, ridged; all shoots twisted and contorted
pest_resistance: Short-lived and brittle; canker and borers
soil_preference: Wet ground; tolerates flooding
description: Every twig curls and corkscrews. Cut stems are sold for flower arranging, and the tree itself rarely lives long.
fun_fact: Every one is a clone. The twisted form does not come true from seed, so all of them are grown from cuttings of the original.

bark_profile: Grey, furrowed with age
pest_resistance: Canker; brittle wood
soil_preference: Wet to moist
description: Willows hybridise so freely that even specialists often stop at the genus. Each bud is wrapped in a single cap-like scale, which no other northern tree has.
fun_fact: Willow bark contains salicin, which people chewed for pain for thousands of years, and which led chemists in the 1800s to the drug that became aspirin.

bark_profile: Deeply furrowed reddish-brown
pest_resistance: Few problems; suckers into thickets
soil_preference: Well-drained, acid, sandy
description: Leaves come in three shapes on the same tree — oval, mitten and three-lobed — and everything about it smells of root beer when broken.
fun_fact: Its root bark flavoured the original root beer, until safrole was banned from food in 1960 and the flavour went synthetic.

bark_profile: Smooth grey, becoming fissured with age
pest_resistance: More resistant to fireblight than true mountain ash
soil_preference: Tolerates urban conditions, salt and wind
description: Leaves are lobed rather than divided, green above and grey-felted beneath. Tough enough for exposed coastal and street planting.
fun_fact: A stable hybrid that breeds true from seed without pollination, so every tree is effectively a clone of its parent.

bark_profile: Smooth shining grey, becoming scaly
pest_resistance: Fire blight; borers; struggles in heat
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; cool sites
description: Rowan, or European mountain ash. Flat heads of white flowers give way to dense clusters of orange-red berries that birds strip quickly.
fun_fact: Rowan was planted by doorways across northern Europe to ward off witches, and the berries make a bitter jelly traditionally eaten with game.

bark_profile: Smooth grey-brown with prominent lenticels
pest_resistance: Fireblight and borers, as with all mountain ashes
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acidic; dislikes heat
description: A hybrid whose leaves are divided at the base and merely lobed at the tip, as though it could not decide. Heavy clusters of red fruit.
fun_fact: Rowan and whitebeam crossed on their own, long before anybody thought to do it deliberately, and the result now comes true from seed — which most hybrids do not.

bark_profile: Smooth grey
pest_resistance: Fire blight
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; cool sites
description: A hybrid mountain ash whose leaves are part-divided, part-whole — an obvious blend of its two parents.
fun_fact: Rowan berries gave their name to sorbic acid, now a common food preservative, first isolated from them in 1859.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: Low, twiggy deciduous shrubs: some flower in arching sprays of white in spring, others in flat pink heads in summer.
fun_fact: Aspirin is named after this genus: meadowsweet, once classed as a Spiraea, was the plant chemists first got salicylic acid from, and the "spir" in aspirin is its old name.

bark_profile: Flaking in grey, orange and cinnamon patches — its best feature
pest_resistance: Few pests; resents transplanting and drought
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained, acid; part shade
description: White, camellia-like flowers in midsummer, orange-red autumn leaves, and bark that flakes in patches of grey, orange and cinnamon.
fun_fact: Linnaeus named the genus for John Stuart, Earl of Bute, and misspelled him. The extra letter has been carried ever since.

bark_profile: Glossy amber-brown, peeling in curls like a birch
pest_resistance: More borer and mildew resistant than shrub lilacs
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates drought and city conditions
description: A small tree lilac with creamy midsummer flower plumes and polished peeling bark that carries it through winter.
fun_fact: Named for Beijing, then called Peking, from where the physician and plant collector Emil Bretschneider sent its seed west in the 1880s.

bark_profile: Polished copper-brown, peeling in curling papery sheets
pest_resistance: More borer and mildew resistant than shrub lilacs
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates drought and city conditions
description: Grown for bark rather than bloom: polished copper peeling in curls, like a cherry that has decided to be a birch.
fun_fact: The copper colour is only the outermost layer: the thin curls peel away every year to show fresh bark underneath.

bark_profile: Glossy reddish-brown with horizontal lenticels, cherry-like
pest_resistance: More borer-resistant than shrub lilacs
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates city conditions
description: A lilac that grows as a real tree, carrying huge plumes of creamy flowers in June, well after the shrubby lilacs have finished.
fun_fact: Lilacs belong to the olive family, along with ash trees and privet, which is why this one's flowers smell more of privet than of lilac.

bark_profile: Glossy reddish-brown with horizontal lenticels, cherry-like
pest_resistance: More borer resistant than shrub lilacs; heat tolerant
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates city conditions and road salt
description: A small street tree carrying huge creamy flower plumes in June, weeks after the shrub lilacs are done. Polished bark carries it through winter.
fun_fact: Flowers younger and more heavily than the species, which is why it is the tree lilac almost everyone plants.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, peeling in thin strips on old stems
pest_resistance: Powdery mildew; lilac borer; scale
soil_preference: Well-drained, neutral to alkaline; full sun
description: A large, many-stemmed shrub with heart-shaped leaves and dense cones of intensely fragrant lilac, purple or white flowers in May. A fixture of old Vermont dooryards.
fun_fact: Brought to New England by the first colonists; a lilac by a cellar hole is often the only sign left that a farmhouse once stood there.

bark_profile: Fibrous red-brown, shallowly furrowed and stringy
pest_resistance: Very few known problems
soil_preference: Wet to average; tolerates standing water and drought
description: Needles are held upright and pressed to the shoot rather than spread flat, giving a narrower, wirier look than bald cypress.
fun_fact: Botanists still argue whether it is a species of its own or a variety of baldcypress. In the wild it keeps to still water, where baldcypress takes the moving kind.

bark_profile: Fibrous, stringy, reddish-brown
pest_resistance: Few known problems; very wind-firm
soil_preference: Wet to moist; also grows well on ordinary soil
description: A deciduous conifer of southern swamps whose feathery foliage turns rusty orange before dropping. Produces knobbly root knees in wet ground.
fun_fact: Its heartwood resists rot so well it was sold as "the wood eternal". Logs that sank in Louisiana swamps a century ago are still pulled up sound and sawn into lumber.

pest_resistance: Varies by species — identify before assuming
description: Dark evergreen shrubs that tolerate deep shade and hard clipping, which is why they fill so many foundation plantings. Flat needles, glossy above and paler beneath.
fun_fact: Every part of a yew is poisonous except the red flesh of the aril, and the seed inside that is among the most toxic parts of all.

bark_profile: Reddish-brown, thin and flaking in scales
pest_resistance: Root rot in wet ground; deer browse heavily
soil_preference: Well-drained; tolerates deep shade and hard pruning
description: The standard hedging yew, hardier than its English parent. All parts except the red aril are poisonous.
fun_fact: A cross of English and Japanese yew made in Massachusetts around 1900, combining English form with Japanese hardiness.

bark_profile: Fibrous reddish-brown, shredding in vertical strips
pest_resistance: Far more deer-resistant than eastern arborvitae; bagworm occasionally
soil_preference: Moist to wet; thrives on limestone
description: A fast, dense screening conifer that deer mostly leave alone — the reason it has replaced eastern arborvitae in new hedges.
fun_fact: Every one descends from a seedling raised in Denmark in 1937. A handful of plants reached the US National Arboretum in 1967, and it spread from there.

bark_profile: Fibrous reddish-brown, shredding in vertical strips
pest_resistance: Deer browse is the main limit here; leaf miner
soil_preference: Moist to wet; thrives on limestone
description: Northern white cedar, growing as flat sprays of scale-like foliage. Cliff-clinging wild trees in Vermont are among the oldest in eastern North America.
fun_fact: French explorers learned from the Iroquois to brew its foliage against scurvy, and named it arborvitae, the tree of life.

bark_profile: Fibrous, shredding
pest_resistance: Deer browse
soil_preference: Moist to wet
description: Dense evergreens with shreddy, fibrous bark, planted everywhere as hedges and screens. Crushed foliage has a sharp, fruity smell.
fun_fact: Every autumn the oldest inner sprays turn brown and drop, which alarms many owners. It is normal shedding, not disease — the outer foliage stays green.

bark_profile: Grey, finely and evenly ridged
pest_resistance: Japanese beetle; aphid honeydew
soil_preference: Deep, moist, fertile; dislikes drought
description: A tall native tree with big, lopsided, heart-shaped leaves, often as wide as a hand. Fragrant early-summer flowers hang from a pale, strap-like wing and hum with bees.
fun_fact: The inner bark strips into strong fibre — bast — which was twisted into rope and woven into mats long before nylon.

bark_profile: Grey, finely and evenly ridged
pest_resistance: Japanese beetle; aphid honeydew
soil_preference: Deep, moist, fertile; dislikes drought
description: A narrow pyramidal basswood, holding the same large leaves and fragrant summer flowers on a crown that fits a street.
fun_fact: Basswood is the favourite wood of hand carvers: soft, pale and so even-grained that it cuts cleanly in any direction.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, finely ridged, dense and even
pest_resistance: Japanese beetle; aphids; sun scald on young bark
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates city air and pruning
description: Small neat heart-shaped leaves and intensely fragrant summer flowers that bees work all day. The standard European street linden.
fun_fact: Berlin's grand avenue, Unter den Linden, is named for the lindens that line it, first planted there in 1647.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, finely and evenly ridged
pest_resistance: Japanese beetle; aphid honeydew drips onto whatever is parked beneath
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates city air and pruning
description: The standard street linden: a straight trunk, an even oval crown and dense uniform branching. Fragrant midsummer bloom that bees work all day.
fun_fact: Linden flowers are dried for lime-blossom tea, a traditional cold remedy across Europe.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly fissured
pest_resistance: Japanese beetle; aphids
soil_preference: Moist, fertile, well-drained
description: A large-leaved linden that flowers earlier than the others, with softly hairy leaf undersides.
fun_fact: Among the longest-lived trees in Europe: bigleaf lindens over a thousand years old stand in village squares in Germany and Austria.

bark_profile: Smooth grey when young, ridging with age
pest_resistance: More Japanese beetle resistant than other lindens
soil_preference: Well-drained; the most heat and drought tolerant linden
description: Leaves flash bright silver-white beneath as they turn in the wind. More tolerant of heat and drought than other lindens.
fun_fact: Dazed and dying bumblebees under its flowers in late summer are a known sight. Research suggests they are starving as the nectar runs out, rather than being poisoned by it.

bark_profile: Grey, ridged, usually with a thicket of burrs and sprouts at the base
pest_resistance: Aphid honeydew is heavy; basal sprouting needs constant removal
soil_preference: Moist, fertile; very tolerant of pruning
description: A natural hybrid of the small- and large-leaved lindens, long planted in European avenues. Often sprouts a thicket of shoots around its base.
fun_fact: It is the "lime" of English country-house avenues: lime is the old British name for linden, nothing to do with the citrus fruit.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, becoming lightly ridged
pest_resistance: Fewer Japanese beetle problems than other lindens
soil_preference: Well-drained; more drought tolerant than other lindens
description: Small, finely cut leaves that are almost maple-like, on a tidy compact crown. Fragrant flowers in early summer.
fun_fact: It grows wild in northern China and Mongolia, which makes it one of the most cold-hardy lindens.

bark_profile: Cinnamon-brown, deeply furrowed with age
pest_resistance: Hemlock woolly adelgid — the defining threat to this species
soil_preference: Cool, moist, acid; shade tolerant, dislikes drought and salt
description: A graceful native conifer with short, flat needles marked with two white stripes beneath, a drooping top, and tiny cones. It grows in cool, shaded ravines.
fun_fact: Hemlock casts the deepest shade of any eastern tree and can wait two centuries in that shade for an opening. The woolly adelgid is now killing it across its range.

bark_profile: Grey, deeply ridged, alternating buff and brown layers in section
pest_resistance: Dutch elm disease — untreated trees are lost; resistant cultivars exist
soil_preference: Moist, deep; tolerates wet and urban conditions
description: The vase-shaped elm that once arched over American main streets, its limbs rising and spreading like a fountain. Lost in vast numbers to Dutch elm disease.
fun_fact: Boston's Liberty Tree, where colonists rallied against British taxes in the 1760s, was an American elm. British soldiers cut it down in 1775.

bark_profile: Grey, deeply ridged in the classic elm pattern
pest_resistance: Selected for Dutch elm disease resistance; still susceptible to elm yellows
soil_preference: Moist, deep; tolerates urban conditions
description: A Dutch elm disease-resistant selection used to restore the classic American elm vase form.
fun_fact: Selected in 1922 for its form, long before Dutch elm disease reached the area — and then found, by luck, to resist it.

bark_profile: Grey, deeply ridged in the classic elm pattern
pest_resistance: Among the most Dutch elm disease resistant selections tested; needs early pruning for structure
soil_preference: Moist, deep; tolerates wet and urban conditions
description: A National Arboretum selection with the highest disease survival in trials, restoring the arching elm form to streets that lost it.
fun_fact: Released in 1995 alongside a second selection, 'New Harmony' — two cultivars rather than one, which matters for a tree whose last monoculture was taken out by a single disease.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, becoming ridged and furrowed
pest_resistance: High resistance to Dutch elm disease
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates drought and urban soils
description: The main source of Dutch elm disease resistance in modern hybrid elms, and the reason elms are being planted on streets again.
fun_fact: Asian elms evolved alongside Dutch elm disease and shrug it off, which is why breeders keep crossing them with the American species.

bark_profile: Smooth grey when young, coarsely ridged with age
pest_resistance: Highly susceptible to Dutch elm disease
soil_preference: Moist, fertile, well-drained
description: Wych elm, with very large rough-textured leaves that feel like sandpaper and a lopsided base typical of elms.
fun_fact: Its leaves are among the largest and roughest of any elm — rough enough to sand wood with, which older books recommended.

bark_profile: Smooth grey when young, coarsely ridged with age
pest_resistance: Highly susceptible to Dutch elm disease
soil_preference: Moist, fertile, well-drained
description: A weeping elm grafted onto a standard, its contorted branches falling straight down into a dome you can stand inside.
fun_fact: Every Camperdown elm descends from one contorted branch found on the Earl of Camperdown's estate in the 1830s, grafted ever since onto a straight stem.

bark_profile: Flaking in irregular patches to show orange, grey and brown beneath
pest_resistance: Good resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle
soil_preference: Wide range; tolerates drought, salt and compaction
description: Mottled bark flakes away in jigsaw patches of orange and grey. Flowers in autumn rather than spring, which is unusual for an elm.
fun_fact: In the warm end of its range it hardly goes dormant at all, carrying green leaves straight through the winter. This far north the cold settles the question for it.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, shallowly furrowed and flaking
pest_resistance: Resists Dutch elm disease but breaks readily in storms
soil_preference: Very adaptable; tolerates drought and poor soil
description: A tough, fast, brittle Asian elm planted for shelterbelts and now weedy across much of the continent.
fun_fact: In northern China its young winged seeds are gathered in spring and eaten, raw or steamed into cakes.

bark_profile: Grey, ridged
pest_resistance: Dutch elm disease
soil_preference: Moist, deep, adaptable
description: Doubly toothed, rough leaves and flat, papery, round seeds. American elm, once the street tree of New England, was nearly wiped out by Dutch elm disease.
fun_fact: Elm rots quickly in the air but lasts almost indefinitely kept wet, so hollowed elm trunks carried London's water for centuries, and some of those pipes are still being dug up intact.

bark_profile: Grey-brown, broken into small blocky plates
pest_resistance: Powdery mildew in crowded sites; viburnum leaf beetle
soil_preference: Moist to dry; tolerates shade and limestone
description: Flat white flower clusters, then blue-black fruit on red stalks that birds strip quickly. Suckers into thickets if left alone.
fun_fact: The fruit sweetens to something like a date after frost, and the buds are long and curved like a crane's bill.

bark_profile: Smooth grey with orange lenticels, flaking to orange patches with age
pest_resistance: Resistant to Dutch elm disease
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates urban conditions
description: An elm relative planted as a disease-resistant substitute for the American elm, with a similar vase shape and flaking orange-grey bark.
fun_fact: Called keyaki in Japan, where it is the traditional wood for taiko drums: the body of a large one is hollowed from a single trunk, so the best come from trees several centuries old.

bark_profile: Smooth grey with orange lenticels, flaking to orange patches with age
pest_resistance: Resistant to Dutch elm disease; a common elm substitute
soil_preference: Moist, well-drained; tolerates urban conditions
description: A strictly columnar zelkova, planted in narrow streets where the vase-shaped species would be far too wide.
fun_fact: Musashino is the plain west of Tokyo, where farmhouses were traditionally sheltered behind planted rows of these trees.
